of pride, no thrill, pleasure, schedule or job that is worth your licence or your life and the lives of your passengers. Complacency kills, and so does being a cowboy.” John Bulmer

                                                          DIFFERENCES                                                    You should also join the circuit overhead and there is no
                                                                                                                         UNICOM.
                                                          Coming To Europe
                                                          First of all, although there are areas where you don't need
                                                          to speak to anyone on the radio, they are very few and far
                                                          between, and at low level, as almost all airspace is
                                                          controlled in some way or another. The transition level is
                                                          also very low, at 3,000 feet (the transition level can
                                                          loosely be called the point at which professional pilots
                                                          start flying on instruments, or without looking through the
                                                          window, so there are strict rules to follow).
                                                          Next, another altimeter setting is typically used for
                                                          takeoffs, landings and operations within the circuit, called
                                                          QFE, which is simply one that gives you a reading of zero
                                                          feet when on the ground. It isn't used in North America
© Phil Croucher Electrocution Technical Publishers 2021




                                                          because many aerodromes are at high elevations and the
                                                          readings would be off the scale. The setting you are used
                                                          to, the nearest aerodrome setting against mean sea level, is
                                                          QNH (QFE is always used in the circuit).
                                                          And what about all those Q codes? They are a hangover
                                                          from the old wireless telegraphy days, and are not
                                                          officially supposed to be used, although everyone does
                                                          (the idea was to use short codes instead of commonly used
                                                          expressions to reduce transmission times. QSY, for
                                                          example, is "changing frequency").

                                                                                                                           less depth of field you have so, in darkness it is hard to see

                                                                                                                           glasses to help. The depth of field is an area either side of
                                                                                                                           the focus point in which everything is sharp. The wider
                                                                                                                           the iris, the shorter this distance is, and vice versa.

                                                                                                                         The heart has 2 pumps*, side by side, each with an atrium

                                                                                                                         inefficiently. This is not considered to be a Good Thing.

                                                          T Y P E S O F A E RO P L A N E
                                                          Aeroplanes are either low, or high wing. The idea behind
                                                          the low wing was to protect the pilot(s) in a crash, since
                                                          the wings would hit the ground first. Later on, it allowed
                                                          for shorter (and therefore lighter) retractable landing gear.
© Phil Croucher Electrocution Technical Publishers 2021




                                                          Aeroplanes can be single- or multi-engined, with fixed or
                                                          retractable undercarriages, if they are landplanes, skis if
                                                          they land on snow, and floats for water:
                                                                                                                            Older aircraft use a truss construction (now mainly used
                                                                                                                            for light training aircraft), or frame and skin, where
                                                                                                                            aluminium or steel tubing is joined in a series of triangular
                                                                                                                            shapes. The idea is that the compression and tension
                                                                                                                            stresses from the bending loads that a fuselage is
                                                                                                                            subjected to are alternately carried by the braces. When
                                                                                                                            they are reversed, the loadings are reversed, so the stresses
                                                                                                                            are spread evenly over the whole structure, avoiding their
                                                                                                                            concentration at any one point.

                                                          made strong enough to take a certain load (mostly tension
                                                          or compression) by itself. Unfortunately, this makes them
                                                          heavy - another disadvantage is that the crossbracing takes

                                                          inside the aircraft, although it suits long, narrow fuselages
© Phil Croucher Electrocution Technical Publishers 2021

                                                                                                                          To be commercially viable, an aircraft must be light, yet
                                                                                                                          strong enough to cope with the forces of flight. For this
                                                                                                                          purpose, materials such as wood, aluminium, titanium,
                                                                                                                          fabric and carbon fibre are used, although pure metals
                                                                                                                          cannot always be used by themselves. For example,
                                                                                                                          although it is light and resists corrosion, aluminium is too
                                                                                                                          soft, so it is mixed with other metals for strength.
                                                          Longerons and stringers are also attachment points for the
                                                          skin, so semi-monocoque construction is better able to
                                                          sustain damage.
                                                          This stressed skin approach is used with wings.

                                                          COMPOSITES                                                     When bulk is needed, a honeycomb construction helps
                                                          Secondary and non-load bearing components can be made          keep things light. This is a framework made of short
                                                          from fibreglass, Kevlar, graphite-based compounds and          hexagonal tubes covered over both open ends by metal or
                                                          composite materials. Cabin floors, for example, are often      laminate sheeting. It is commonly used in cabin floors, in
                                                          made from an aluminium and fibreglass honeycomb that           a sandwich, with aluminium, KevlarTM or NomexTM.
                                                          is sandwiched between aluminium sheeting.
                                                          Technically, a “composite” is a material with two or more
                                                          distinct constituents. Although concrete fits the
                                                          description, in aviation, the word is taken to mean fibres
                                                          embedded in some sort of resin (e.g. epoxy), and they are
                                                          very strong in tension (KevlarTM is one example, but so
                                                          are carbon and glass). They can also be moulded into
                                                          weird shapes consistent with the load, plus they are
                                                          lighter, resistant to corrosion, and flexible. However,
                                                          composites can be eroded easily by hail or sand, and may
                                                          be difficult to repair. Not being electrically conductive,
© Phil Croucher Electrocution Technical Publishers 2021




                                                          they also need arrangements for bonding, and for
                                                          lightning conduction. The big difference from metal is a
                                                          more gradual deterioration profile.

                                                                                                                                  • the number of landings.

                                                          large increase in drag, so it is mainly used for approach

                                                          marginally reduced, to around 14, due to the same
                                                          boundary layer separation.
                                                          A slotted flap has a gap between the trailing edge of the
                                                          wing and its leading edge, which acts like a venturi to let
© Phil Croucher Electrocution Technical Publishers 2021




                                                          air flow from the high pressure area beneath the wing to
                                                          the low-pressure area above it.
                                                          The additional kinetic energy makes the air flow further
                                                          back along the upper surface of the flap before separating.
                                                          This increases CLmax by about 65% and increases the
                                                          stalling angle of attack by 1 or 2º. The drag produced is
                                                          much less than with plain or split flaps, so it can be used
                                                          in a limited way during takeoff as well as landing. In
                                                          summary, a slotted flap increases CLmax by increasing the
                                                          camber of the aerofoil and re-energising the airflow by
                                                          preventing it from breaking away.

                                                               • Angle Of Attack. This is the angle between the                NEWTON’S LAWS
                                                                 oncoming air or relative wind, and the chord line of
                                                                 the wing,                                                     Aside from inventing the catflap (true!), Sir Isaac Newton
                                                                                                                               (influenced by Kepler and Galileo, amongst others),
                                                                                                                               formulated three laws of motion that govern material
                                                                                                                               bodies, which are also relevant to flight:

                                                                                                                               The First Law
                                                                                                                               As first presented by Galileo, a body will continue to
                                                                                                                               move with a constant velocity unless a force is applied to
                                                                                                                               it, as bodies have a natural tendency to maintain their
                                                                                                                               current state of motion. It is a force resisting change that
                                                                                                                               gives a body the tendency to remain at rest, or carry on
                                                                                                                               with what it's doing - in other words, not to change its
                                                                                                                               present state (but see Momentum, below, about stopping).
                                                                   The most efficient angle of attack is that where you
                                                                   get the best ratio of lift to drag, which is a resistance   To do its work, air must possess the property of inertia.
© Phil Croucher Electrocution Technical Publishers 2021




                                                                   (friction) to anything flying through air, and which        Inertia should not be confused with Momentum, as even
                                                                   also requires power to overcome.                            bodies at rest have inertia. Both can add stress to the
                                                                                                                               materials used in aircraft, as found with wings that flex on
                                                                                                                               takeoff or landing. When mass changes, inertia changes,
                                                                                                                               too, as it is proportional to mass.
                                                                                                                               Put more simply, an object in a steady state is neither
                                                                                                                               accelerating nor decelerating (although it might be
                                                                                                                               moving) and you must apply a force to make it move or
                                                                                                                               change direction (or if you observe an acceleration, there
                                                                                                                               must be a force behind it). As air has mass, it is capable of
                                                                                                                               applying force.

                                                          The Boundary L ayer
                                                          Up to a certain critical airspeed, air flowing over or
                                                          around a body close to the surface will hug its shape and
                                                          flow in a laminar fashion, after which it breaks up to form
                                                          vortices that may interfere with any lifting action.
                                                          Airflow is laminar if it follows a smooth path while it is
© Phil Croucher Electrocution Technical Publishers 2021




                                                          accelerating and its parallel layers do not interfere with
                                                          each other. That is, it is non-turbulent, and its layers have   You get one simply by cutting off the bottom half, at
                                                          different velocities.                                           which point there will be a tendency for what remains of
                                                                                                                          the sphere to move up due to the reduced pressure on top.
                                                          Airflow tends to follow the outline of a body because its
                                                          pressure reduces as it speeds up on its way round. It wants
                                                          to follow a straight line (after Newton’s First Law), but it
                                                          cannot, so the same pressure cannot be exerted on the
                                                          surface it is travelling over. A lower static pressure is
                                                          therefore created, relative to the air at atmospheric
                                                          pressure further out from the body, and the air flow is
                                                          pushed against the surface.

                                                                                                                            CAMBER
                                                                                                                            The word camber is popularly used to mean the curvature
                                                                                                                            of the upper surface of an aerofoil.
                                                                                                                            A positively cambered aerofoil has the greatest curvature
                                                                                                                            on its upper surface, and a negatively cambered one has it
                                                                                                                            on the lower surface. The maximum camber is referred to
                                                                                                                            as “the camber”, because it is the only dimension worth
                                                                                                                            bothering about, being there to smooth out and accelerate
                                                          It can be changed in many ways - collecting ice will alter        the airflow over the upper surface. Increasing the camber
                                                                                                                            concentrates the airflow to make it speed up to assist the
© Phil Croucher Electrocution Technical Publishers 2021




                                                          its shape and therefore its lift producing characteristics,
                                                          and make it heavier. In other words, if ice or snow, or any       reduction of pressure.
                                                          other contamination collects on an aerofoil, there is a
                                                          reduction of lift, and the extra weight makes things worse.
                                                          The largest ice build-up will be on the frontal areas of the
                                                          aircraft, typically where the stagnation point is located.
                                                          If you factor in the extra weight, you will need more
                                                          power, plus you will get a lower stalling angle of attack
                                                          and a higher stalling speed, discussed later.

                                                          The aspect ratio of a wing is the
                                                          relationship between its length and
                                                          width. Aerofoils can have equal
                                                          surface areas (and hence roughly the
                                                          same lift production) but different aspect ratios,
                                                          depending on what they were designed for. Glider wings
                                                          have high aspect ratios.

                                                          EFFECTS OF POWER
                                                          Stall speeds are usually given for power off, or at least
                                                          with the engines at idle. Leaving the power on will
                                                          provide a lower stalling speed (assuming no change in
                                                          weight and configuration), but there may also be a more
                                                          violent wing drop at the stall, especially with single-
                                                          engined propeller driven aircraft.

                                                          The Spin
                                                          In a spin, the downgoing wing has stalled, and its angle of
                                                          attack as it drops is increased, so it drops further as the
                                                          damping effect you would get from normal airflow is not
                                                          there - instead, the wing destroys its own lift and any
                                                          attempt to raise it with the ailerons will make it worse. At
                                                          the same time, the increased drag creates a yaw, leading
                                                          you into autorotation, often called the incipient spin. The
                                                          aeroplane is unstable and undamped. Meanwhile, the
                                                          upgoing wing reduces its angle of attack, but still creates
                                                          more lift and turns the aircraft further in. Once the rolling
                                                          and yawing motions become self-sustaining, the aircraft is
                                                          spinning and both wings are stalled!
                                                          Recovery comes from reducing the rolling moment and/or
                                                          trying to yaw the other way. Of the two, the yawing
© Phil Croucher Electrocution Technical Publishers 2021




                                                          moment is the more important, but the rudder (the normal
                                                          yaw control) is not the only game in town. First, set idle
                                                          power, then full opposite rudder, push the control column
                                                          forward until the spin stops, keeping the ailerons in the
                                                          neutral position. You may need to use the ailerons,
                                                          depending on the type.

                                                          The pitching, rolling and yawing planes translate to                   Static Stability
                                                          longitudinal, lateral and directional stability, respectively.         This is the initial (or primary) ability to return to a desired
                                                                                                                                 attitude or its short term reaction:
                                                                                                                                     • An aircraft that uses a restoring moment to return to
                                                                                                                                       its original position after a disturbance is statically
                                                                                                                                       stable, or has positive static stability (the only
                                                                                                                                       condition that leads to dynamic stability).
                                                                                                                                     • An aircraft that moves further away from its original
                                                                                                                                       position is statically unstable, or has negative static
                                                                                                                                       stability. This is usually only possible if energy is
                                                                                                                                       added to the mix, such as mishandling the controls,
                                                                                                                                       so it is rare. A statically unstable aeroplane is never
                                                                                                                                       dynamically stable.
                                                                                                                                     • An aircraft that takes up a new position away from
                                                                                                                                       the first position without needing a force to maintain
© Phil Croucher Electrocution Technical Publishers 2021




                                                                                                                                       it is neutrally stable.

                                                                                                                                 Dynamic Stability
                                                                                                                                 Dynamic stability reflects the long term (secondary)
                                                                                                                                 ability of a statically stable aircraft to settle down after a
                                                                                                                                 series of oscillations (the aircraft must be statically stable
                                                                                                                                 before it can oscillate at all). That is, a statically stable
                                                                                                                                 aircraft will start on its way back to where it came from,
                                                                                                                                 but overshooting brings it into dynamic stability, which is
                                                                                                                                 governed by mass or inertia.

                                                          The end result is you roll the wrong way, or at least the

                                                          normal flight envelope but, when in extreme situations,
                                                          such as in a steep turn, near the stall (and don't forget that
                                                          a stall can happen at any speed with the wrong angle of

                                                          ailerons too abruptly, especially when the lifting wing
                                                          stalls and puts you in a spin, which is just what you don't
                                                          want at 200 feet (remember the aileron's purpose is to
                                                          temporarily increase the angle of attack).

                                                          When taking off near a thunderstorm, and the headwind
                                                          component decreases sharply and/or becomes a tailwind
                                                          component (an energy loss), the groundspeed remains
                                                          constant (inertia again) but the airspeed decreases sharply,
                                                          with an equally sharp loss of lift.

                                                          ACTIONS TO BE TAKEN
                                                          Usually, delaying the landing or takeoff is best -
                                                          microbursts only last for 5 minutes anyway. If you
                                                          encounter a windshear after taking off, maintain the gear
                                                          and flap position until terrain clearance is assured.
                                                          If there is an unexpected loss of airspeed, the
                                                          recommended actions are:
                                                               • Increase power rapidly (full go-around if needed).
                                                               • Raise the nose to check the descent.
© Phil Croucher Electrocution Technical Publishers 2021




                                                               • Coordinate power and pitch.
                                                               • Be prepared to carry out a missed approach.
                                                          For downbursts near thunderstorms:
                                                               • Use the maximum power available as soon as
                                                                 possible.
                                                               • Adopt a pitch angle of about 15° and hold it. Do not
                                                                 chase the airspeed.
                                                          Refer to the stick shaker when holding or increasing pitch
                                                          attitude, easing the back pressure as required to obtain and
                                                          hold a slightly lower attitude.

                                                          flows in the reverse direction.                               Problem 1 is that the generator is driven by an engine,
                                                                                                                        which can run at different speeds, and Problem 2 is that
                                                                                                                        the electrical loads may change, so the next step is to vary
                                                                                                                        the field current of a generator in sympathy with the

                                                                                                                        to maintain it at a constant value. If the generator’s output
                                                                                                                        is low, it will increase the field strength so, if a voltage
                                                                                                                        regulator increases current through field windings, the
                                                                                                                        intensity of the field increases, as does the output voltage.

                                                                                                                        output voltage. In this case, the voltage regulator acts as a

                                                                                                                        variable resistor between the external field connection and
                                                                                                                        the ground. A reverse current relay between the generator
                                                                                                                        and the bus stops the battery discharging through the
                                                                                                                        generator, putting the generator online again as soon as its
                                                                                                                        voltage rises above the battery’s. It is open when
                                                                                                                        everything is switched off.

                                                          released from fuel) and work got out from an engine (shaft     output) of a 4-stroke aircraft engine is 30%. About 40% is
                                                          power). As there will always be heat losses through            lost through the exhaust gases, and another large chunk
                                                          conduction, friction and waste from the exhaust, no            through the cooling mechanism. Although allowing the
                                                          engine is even close to 100% efficient, especially when        engine to run hotter will stop some of this loss, the
                                                          you consider that any cooling system would waste further       lubricating oil and other parts need to be kept within

                                                          THERMAL EFFICIENCY                                             A piston engine keeps whatever efficiency it has at almost
                                                          This measures how much heat energy is converted to             any power setting because each combustion cycle
                                                          kinetic energy, expressed as a percentage.                     produces more or less the same amount of heat. As their
                                                          The First Law of Thermodynamics states that energy may         power is altered by changing RPM or manifold pressure,
                                                          be changed from one form to another, but not created or        they can run reasonably well at partial power.
                                                          destroyed. As far as engines are concerned, it means that
© Phil Croucher Electrocution Technical Publishers 2021




                                                          heat and mechanical work are mutually convertible, and
                                                          that the rate of exchange is constant and measurable.
                                                          However, the second law says (more or less) that: Heat
                                                          flows from a hot substance to a cold one unaided, but
                                                          energy from an external source is needed for it to flow the
                                                          other way. That is, you might be able to convert most of
                                                          your work into heat, but turning heat into work will incur
                                                          serious losses, which is another way of saying that
                                                          engines are grossly inefficient - if it were otherwise,
                                                          exhausts would be cold!

                                                                                                                        THE BOURDON TUBE
© Phil Croucher Electrocution Technical Publishers 2021




                                                                                                                        The most commonly used pressure sensor was invented
                                                                                                                        by French watchmaker Eugene Bourdon in 1849, in which
                                                                                                                        a C-shaped elliptical hollow spring tube is sealed at one
                                                                                                                        end, with the other end connected to a source of pressure.
                                                                                                                        The pressure differential from the inside to the outside
                                                                                                                        makes the tube change from an elliptical to a more
                                                                                                                        circular shape, and to straighten out, rather like an
                                                                                                                        uncoiling hose. Which way it moves is determined by the
                                                                                                                        curvature of the tubing, as the inside radius is slightly
                                                                                                                        shorter than that on the outside, and the ratio between the
                                                                                                                        major and minor axes depends on what sensitivity you
                                                                                                                        need - the larger the ratio, the greater it is.
                                                          EASA Private Pilot Studies                                                                                             6-4

                                                          thickness and the radius of the curvature.                      The term manometer is often used to refer
                                                                                                                          specifically to liquid column hydrostatic
                                                                                                                          instruments. These consist of a vertical

                                                                                                                          exposed to different pressures, with the
                                                                                                                          difference in fluid height being proportional

                                                                                                                          However, the simplest design is a closed-end

                                                                                                                          applied pressure multiplied by the area of the
                                                                                                                          bore will force the liquid downwards until,
                                                          The end result is that a specific pressure causes movement      eventually, the two levels will stand the same

                                                          tube returns to its original shape. To do this, the material
                                                          used requires a form of heat treating (spring tempering) to     bore and the density of the liquid, you can calculate

                                                                                                                        Various methods can be used to make an instrument over-

                                                          FLIGHT INSTRUMENTS                                                As mentioned, instruments cover four areas of aircraft
                                                                                                                            operation:
                                                          Flight instruments are grouped in a T arrangement.

                                                                                                                            A primary instrument is one which gives instant and
                                                                                                                            constant readouts (also called direct). A secondary
                                                                                                                            instrument is one that you have to deduce things from,

                                                                                                                            must have changed (you might also say that the altimeter

                                                          below that, and the airspeed indicator at the top left with       only indicate that a change is taking place.

                                                          The idea is to have the most important instruments as             pitch, bank and power.

                                                          Altimetry is the science of measuring vertical distances in
                                                          the atmosphere. The pressure decrease with altitude
                                                          depends on gravity and air density (hydrostatic balance).
                                                              pressure = g x density x height diff
                                                          As vertical pressure variation follows the general gas
                                                          laws, if you know the pressure on the ground and that at
                                                          your height, you can work out your distance from the
                                                          surface. 1 hPa is equal to 27 feet in the lower atmosphere.
                                                                   The word height refers to the vertical distance
                                                                   from a particular datum, usually the surface of an
                                                                   airfield (QFE, as used in Europe, is the airfield
                                                          datum pressure, which makes the altimeter read your
© Phil Croucher Electrocution Technical Publishers 2021




                                                          height above the airfield).
                                                          Altitude means distance above sea level, so the aircraft
                                                          below has a height of 1000 feet (above the aerodrome, or                  Pressure corrections are applied between the ISA
                                                          QFE) and an altitude of 1500 feet (above the sea, or                      Standard Pressure Datum (1013 hPa) and the
                                                          QNH).The difference is the elevation of the aerodrome.                    QNH datum. Temperature corrections are only
                                                                                                                          applied above the QFE datum, or to the air that actually
                                                          Elevation is the vertical distance of a point on the Earth's
                                                                                                                          exists, above the airfield elevation.
                                                          surface from mean sea level. Indicated altitude is what is
                                                          shown on the dial at the current altimeter setting.
                                                          Calibrated altitude is the indicated altitude corrected for
                                                          instrument and position error.

                                                                                                   6     Airspeed Indicator




                                                          A I RS P E E D I N D I C A T O R                    022 02 06       The needle is connected to the capsule through the usual
                                                                                                                              suitable linkage.
                                                          We need to know the speed of flight through the air for
                                                          performance and structural reasons, and navigation.
                                                          To find airspeed, you need to compare the general
                                                          pressure outside the aircraft (the static pressure) with the
                                                          pressure created from its movement through the air, so
                                                          this instrument is connected to both the static and pitot
                                                          pressure systems.
                                                          The ASI is similar to the altimeter inside, except that the
                                                          capsule is fed directly with pitot pressure, and its size will
                                                          vary in direct proportion to any increase or decrease. As           Dynamic pressure varies with the square of the airspeed.
                                                          the capsule expands under the pressure of the ram air,              The combination of static and dynamic pressure is the
                                                          static air in the case can escape through the static port. If it    stagnation pressure, because airflow is being brought to
                                                          were otherwise, the capsule would not be able to expand.            rest inside the pitot tube, or stagnating.
© Phil Croucher Electrocution Technical Publishers 2021




                                                          The ASI is a pressure gauge with its dial marked in knots
                                                          or mph instead of psi so, when it sees 76.2 lbs per square
                                                          foot at sea level, it will indicate 150 kts, regardless of
                                                          whether the pressure arises from a low speed in high
                                                          density air or the opposite (this would have to be corrected
                                                          to find TAS at altitude). It captures total pressure (inside
                                                          the capsule) then subtracts static pressure (outside) to get
                                                          dynamic pressure, which is proportional to forward speed,
                                                          so differential pressure is measured.

                                                                                                                              Because the atmosphere gets less dense as you climb, the
                                                                                                                              IAS must be corrected. The rate is 1.75% per 1000 feet.

                                                                                                6     Gyroscopes




                                                          GYROSCOPES                                        022 04 01     A gyroscope is a heavy rotating mass on a vertical or
                                                                                                                          horizontal axis*, suspended in inner and outer gimbals

                                                          G        yros are used in aircraft to establish three
                                                                   reference planes, namely Pitch, Roll and Yaw but,
                                                                   as they only have two reference rings (or gimbals -
                                                          see Types Of Gyroscope, below), we need more than one
                                                                                                                          which are in frames. Its operation depends on the
                                                                                                                          resistance to deflection of a spinning wheel or disc, and
                                                                                                                          only its Centre of Gravity remains fixed in space. The
                                                                                                                          gyro is otherwise free to turn in any direction around it.
                                                          to get the information we need. In fact, three instruments
                                                                                                                          *A gyroscope’s axis of rotation defines its orientation. A
                                                          are usually under gyroscopic influence, the Attitude
                                                                                                                          vertical gyro has its axis in Earth Vertical (as opposed to
                                                          Indicator (artificial horizon), Directional Gyroscopic
                                                                                                                          aircraft vertical) and a horizontal gyro is in Earth
                                                          Indicator (DGI) and Turn Indicator or Coordinator. The
                                                                                                                          Horizontal, but aligned with North.
                                                          first two are typically suction-powered and the last by
                                                          electricity, but many are now all electric.
                                                          Gyros (and accelerometers) are also called inertial
                                                          sensors because they use resistance to changes in
                                                          momentum to sense angular (gyro) and linear motion
                                                          (accelerometer).
© Phil Croucher Electrocution Technical Publishers 2021




                                                          The Earth itself is a gyroscope. Around the Equator it
                                                          spins at around 1000 knots, as opposed to the more typical
                                                          250 knots for man-made gyroscopes. As such, it is able to
                                                          maintain its position in space to within 1° of the North
                                                          Star. The problem for us is that we need the gyros to
                                                          maintain a position with reference to the Earth, hence the
                                                          various correction mechanisms described later.

                                                          Underneath the indicator is a steel ball (or similar) in a                     TURN AND BANK (SLIP) INDICATOR

                                                          doesn’t affect the rate of turn).                                              of the horizontal small aircraft in the artificial

                                                                                                                                         since it is only sensitive to yaw, which is what is measured

                                                          When a turn is balanced*, centrifugal force offsets the pull

                                                          indicator marks.
                                                          In a slip, where the rate of turn is not enough for the angle
                                                          of bank, the centrifugal force will be weak and the ball
                                                          will fall to the inside of the turn.
                                                          In a skid, the turn is too fast, so the extra centrifugal force
                                                          displaces the ball more, to the outside of the turn.

                                                          DESTINATION, EET, SAR, ALTERNATE
                                                          In Box 16, use the ICAO code. For VFR, the EET is from
                                                          takeoff until overhead the destination (including
                                                          intermediate stops, although these are naturally rare with
                                                          IFR). For IFR, it’s to the IAF. Use your own SAR time, up
                                                          to 24 hours after ETA.
                                                          A takeoff alternate is required when the weather at the
                                                          departure aerodrome is at or below landing minima, or
                                                          you cannot return to it for other reasons. If you need one
                                                          that doesn't have an ICAO ID, use ZZZZ, with the details
                                                          in Box 18 after /ALTN. If you land at another destination,
                                                          you must inform the flight planned destination within 30
                                                          minutes of the planned ETA.

                                                          OTHER INFORMATION
© Phil Croucher Electrocution Technical Publishers 2021




                                                          Use 0 if there is nothing to add. RMK/ means Remarks.

                                                          SUPPLEMENTAL INFORMATION
                                                          Fuel endurance (total usable fuel) in hours and minutes
                                                          goes in Box 19. You can use TBN if you don’t know how
                                                          many passengers you will have. Place an X through the U
                                                          and V if you don’t have the VHF and UHF emergency
                                                          frequencies (243 & 121.5 MHz). Cross out the survival
                                                          equipment you don't have, and add with whom the arrival
                                                          report will be filed. Finally, include your name and licence
                                                          number, and the person to be notified if SAR is initiated.

                                                          VMC Vi sibility & Dist ance From Cl oud                           CLASS A AIRSPACE
                                                          A VFR flight must be operated in conditions of visibility         This is the most restrictive, requiring the most
                                                          and distance from clouds equal to or greater than those           experienced pilots. Except for gliders, all flights are IFR -
                                                          given in the table below.                                         you may not convert to VFR.

                                                                                                                            CLASS B AIRSPACE
                                                                                                                            You must be clear of cloud, with visibility at least 8 km (5
                                                                                                                            km below 10,000' AMSL). In UK, Class B airspace only
                                                                                                                            exists above FL 245.

                                                                                                                            CLASS C, D OR E AIRSPACE
                                                                                                                            You must be at least 1500 m horizontally and 1000 feet
                                                                                                                            vertically from cloud in visibility of at least 8 km (5 km
                                                                                                                            below 10,000' AMSL). Class C airspace does not as yet
                                                                                                                            exist in UK.
© Phil Croucher Electrocution Technical Publishers 2021




                                                                                                                            CLASS F & G AIRSPACE
                                                                                                                            Above 3,000 ft AMSL, or 1000 AGL, whichever is
                                                                                                                            higher, you must be at least 1500 m horizontally and 1000
                                                                                                                            feet vertically from cloud in visibility at least 8 km (5 km
                                                                                                                            below 10,000' AMSL*). Class F is advisory airspace in
                                                                                                                            which ATC is available but not mandatory, and Class G is
                                                          OVERWATER                                                         totally uncontrolled.
                                                          Flight shall not be conducted overwater out of sight of
                                                          land when the flight visibility is less than that for the
                                                          appropriate airspace, and in any case when it is less than
                                                          1500 m. The minimum cloudbase shall be 600 feet.

                                                          APPROACH LIGHTING                                                  The simple system is a row of lights on the extended
                                                          Approach lighting uses cross bars and centreline lighting,         centre line for at least 420 m from the threshold, with a
                                                          with strobes for when background lighting is high.                 row as a crossbar 18 or 30 m long, 300 m from the
                                                                                                                             threshold, starting up to 500 m before the threshold.
                                                          Runway lighting works backwards from the threshold. It
                                                          has a purpose other than to show you the way in at night -
                                                          it's also meant to help you transition to the visual after
                                                          emerging from the murk during an approach. There are
                                                          various designs for various purposes, shown below.
                                                          S IMPLE
                                                          These are for non-precision runways, although they can

                                                          a Cat I system. They can also be used for Code 3 or 4 non-
                                                          instrument runways intended for night use.
                                                          Simple systems can be single source or barrette (a barrette
                                                          is 3 or more aeronautical ground lights closely spaced).

                                                          Adding water vapour to air makes it less dense because
                                                          the molecular weight is lower (dry air is 29 - water vapour
                                                          is 18). On cold days, humidity is less of a problem
                                                          because cold air holds less vapour. A relative humidity of
                                                          90% at 70°F means twice as much than at 50°F.

                                                                                       10    The Centre Of Gravity




                                                                                                                     THE CENTRE OF GRAVITY
                                                                                                                     The Centre of Gravity of an object is a point where its
                                                                                                                     weight (or gravitational attraction) passes through, or
                                                                                                                     where its mass is concentrated, so all the forces involved
                                                                                                                     act parallel to the gravity vector (OK, they actually point
                                                                                                                     towards the centre of the Earth, but that is so far away you
                                                                                                                     may as well regard them as being parallel). When
                                                                                                                     stationary on the ground, the total weight of an aircraft
                                                                                                                     will act vertically through the Centre of Gravity.
                                                                                                                     The C of G could also be described as the average location
                                                                                                                     of an object’s weight force, or its point of balance, around
                                                                                                                     which an autopilot will control an aircraft. It is normally
                                                                                                                     referenced to the longitudinal axis.
                                                                                                                     The location of the C of G depends on the object’s shape,
                                                                                                                     density and the external gravitational field. If a vertical
© Phil Croucher Electrocution Technical Publishers 2021




                                                                                                                     line through the C of G lies outside the base on which the
                                                                                                                     object relies for support, it will overturn, unless you do
                                                                                                                     something to counterbalance the force:

                                                                                        Purchased by Andrew Done, andrewdone@fastmail.com #20310022

                                                                                              10      The Centre Of Gravity

                                                          from it - the difference is compensated for by each one’s           *If it is too far aft, especially behind the C of P, the aircraft

                                                          THE LOAD                                                         Here are the relevant definitions:
                                                          Generally, actual weights must be used, meaning that you            • The Basic Empty Mass is that in the Weight and
                                                          must physically weigh your passengers and cargo.                      Centre of Gravity Schedule, which is established by
                                                                                                                                weighing before the machine is used. It is the mass
                                                                                                                                of the empty aircraft, plus integral equipment (fire
                                                                                                                                extinguishers, etc.) and fluids in closed systems
                                                                                                                                (unusable fuel and full operating fluids).
                                                                                                                              • The Dry Operating Mass is the BEM plus any
                                                                                                                                items for a specific type of flight, including the
                                                                                                                                pilot(s), their baggage, unusable fuel and oil,
                                                                                                                                paperwork, etc. (this used to be the APS Weight).
                                                                                                                              • Maximum (Structural) TakeOff Mass (MTOM).
                                                                                                                                The maximum allowable total mass at the start of
                                                                                                                                takeoff. A structural limitation in the flight manual
                                                                                                                                that may not be exceeded.
© Phil Croucher Electrocution Technical Publishers 2021




                                                                                                                              • Maximum (Structural) Landing Mass (MLM). The
                                                                                                                                maximum permissible total mass on landing under
                                                                                                                                normal circumstances. A flight manual restriction
                                                                                                                                that may not be exceeded at any time. It helps to
                                                                                                                                prevent the impact with the ground being
                                                                                                                                transmitted through the undercarriage to the rest of
                                                                                                                                the aircraft, which can only happen if the weight is
                                                                                                                                kept within limits (it also assists in reducing
                                                                                                                                downward velocity). This weight may very well be
                                                                                                                                restricted performance-wise in a similar way to
                                                                                                                                Takeoff Mass, and could equally be a factor in
                                                                                                                                further reducing your payload at the start of a flight.

                                                                                                                                   Theory Of Operation
                                                                                                                                   The radiation from a conventional VOR (CVOR) is a
                                                                                                                                   complex horizontally polarised VHF wave. Because the
                                                                                                                                   signal is frequency and amplitude modulated, it is classed
                                                                                                                                   as an A9W signal (Doppler VOR, mentioned later, has its
                                                                                                                                   modulations the other way round).

                                                                                                                                       Distance Measuring Equipment is secondary radar, but in
                                                                           Class       Bearing   Position                              reverse. It measures the time difference between paired
                                                                             A          œ2¬       5 nm                                 pulses sent from an aircraft being received back (on
                                                                             B          œ5¬       20 nm

                                                                             C          œ10¬      50 nm
